reasons: The repo has no pyproject.toml, requirements file or tools/ directory. Choosing argparse adds no dependency, so there is nothing to install, pin or upgrade.
The tool is small, with three subcommands. argparse's add_subparsers covers that directly.

One person will maintain it for years. The standard library ships with Python 3.11 and rarely makes breaking changes. click and typer are third-party packages that need version pinning and occasional upgrades. typer also depends on click.

The strongest point against argparse is that click and typer need less boilerplate and give nicer help output and shell completion. For three subcommands the extra code is small, and a dependency that must be maintained for years costs more than that code.

evidence.claim: The repo has no dependency manifest and no tools/ directory, so there is no existing dependency or convention to match.
evidence.source: Glob for pyproject.toml, requirements*.txt, setup.py, setup.cfg and tools/* in /private/var/folders/jx/81xz9_xj7x31h6mwxd7qrlj40000gn/T/free-hands-lab-r2-r04/repo returned no files

risks: I did not fetch the argparse, click or typer documentation. The claims about argparse subparsers, typer's dependence on click, and the stability of the standard library come from my own knowledge, not from a source I checked.
If the tool later grows to many nested subcommands, or needs rich completion or prompts, click would be the better fit and migrating would cost some effort.
I could not see whether the repo is meant to use third-party packages. The brief lists no files.
would_change_if: The repo already depends on click or typer, the tool is expected to grow well beyond three subcommands, or the maintainer wants completion and prompts out of the box.
